competitors.compliance: Every diner follows the same path whatever the score, and the private note sits beside the public review rather than replacing it. Photo rules forbid people (staff privacy), menus, empty plates and promotional material; staff full names are discouraged in text. Restaurants do not see the diner's email.
standoutIdeas: Private note as a companion to the public review in one form: the compliant way to offer a private channel. It maps to RepKey's private feedback shown next to the Google action.
Verified-visit framing ('only diners who booked and honored a reservation') builds trust.
Editing and deleting are the guest's rights, matching RepKey's correct/withdraw receipt.
antiPatterns: Sign-in wall and a long form, which is slow for an at-table moment.
The review arrives hours later by email, after the moment has passed.

competitors.name: Resy post-visit rating
competitors.category: Reservation platform closed-loop private rating
competitors.guestFlow: 'A few hours after their reservation is complete, guests are sent an email' asking for 1-5 stars and a comment. Third-party summaries mention factor chips (Food, Service, Vibe, Other); the vendor blog does not confirm them. The rating is private: it is 'emailed to you every morning instead of being posted on the internet for all to see'. No public-platform redirect is documented.
competitors.mobileAnatomy: Not observed. Inferred to be an email with a star row, plus a lightweight web form with a comment field and factor chips.
competitors.visualStyle: Resy platform editorial style (not observed in this pass).
competitors.adminBuilder: Not documented beyond the reservation system.
competitors.analytics: A morning email to the restaurant with each rating in context: 'exactly what time the party was seated, its table number, its server's name'. Guest Info Trends appears in Advanced Analytics.
competitors.compliance: Closed-loop private feedback with no Google steering, so no gating.
standoutIdeas: Closed-loop private rating is exactly RepKey's first step. Resy shows restaurants value it on its own.
Attach context to each rating (for RepKey, the portal or placement, since RepKey has no reservation data).
A morning digest cadence.
antiPatterns: No path to public review at all, so the owner gets no reputation lift.

competitors.name: TheFork (TheFork Manager)
competitors.category: European reservation platform verified reviews, 10-point scale
competitors.guestFlow: Only verified diners who booked through TheFork can review. Scores are out of 10, with sub-ratings for food, service and ambience/setting (vendor blog; the sub-ratings are corroborated only by third-party summaries). The request comes as a follow-up email; the vendor also suggests 'a friendly in-person reminder at the end of a meal'. The live review page returned no text to the reader (client-rendered), so it was not observed.
competitors.mobileAnatomy: Not observed.
competitors.visualStyle: Not observed in this pass. Scores are shown publicly as x/10 averages.
competitors.adminBuilder: TheFork Manager can 'share your 10/10 reviews (including the rating and comment) on Instagram or other social media channels in just three easy clicks'.
competitors.analytics: Review pages per restaurant; details not captured.
competitors.compliance: Verified-diner model. Resharing only 10/10 reviews to social media is selective display, not solicitation; in the EU it is fine as long as it is not presented as representative (UCPD 23b 'misrepresenting consumer reviews').
standoutIdeas: A 10-point scale is common in European restaurant culture (TheFork, Booking-style), but RepKey's 1-5 matches Google's mental model better.
A shareable review card for social media is a pride-driver for owners (a possible future admin feature, not guest-facing).
antiPatterns: Showing only 10/10 reviews in marketing could mislead if presented as the overall sentiment.

competitors.name: Tablein
competitors.category: EU reservation system with day-after feedback email and high-score redirect
competitors.guestFlow: 'The day after each reservation happens, the Tablein system automatically sends an email to our guests with a request to review our food, service, ambience, and cleanliness, plus add an optional comment.' Then: 'If the review is very high, the guest is now automatically invited to leave one more review on Google, Tripadvisor or Facebook.' Reviews are also 'published on the restaurant's website, in the reservations section (powered by Tablein)'.
competitors.mobileAnatomy: Not observed. The vendor says 'Sharing their experience in our restaurant takes only a single click' (likely a star row in the email that deep-links to the form, inferred).
competitors.visualStyle: Not observed.
competitors.adminBuilder: Automatic; no setup described.
competitors.analytics: Product tour: a 'Latest feedback & ratings' panel. Each review is tied to the reservation (time, dishes, server, cook).
competitors.compliance: The high-score-only invitation to Google, Tripadvisor or Facebook is review gating and conflicts with Tripadvisor's rule that 'the user interface and experience for submitting positive and negative reviews must be identical'.
standoutIdeas: Cleanliness as an explicit dimension, useful in BG/EU hospitality.
A widget that republishes first-party reviews on the owner's website (a future idea; it needs EU Art. 7(6) disclosure of how reviews are verified).
antiPatterns: An invitation to public platforms that only fires for high scores.
Feedback arrives the next day by email, disconnected from the venue moment.

competitors.name: HappyOrNot (Smiley Terminal, Smiley Sign, Smiley Link, Smiley Digital)
competitors.category: Four-face feedback kiosks and their QR/NFC mobile-web counterparts
competitors.guestFlow: Scan the QR or tap the NFC chip on a Smiley Sign (poster, sticker, table talker, table tent, wobbler, or an outdoor Foamex board); it 'goes live as soon as it is posted'. No app or login. One location-specific question (for example 'How was your check-out process?'), then four smileys with no neutral option, then a follow-up with options tailored to green or red answers, then optional open text, then submit and thank-you. Smiley Sign can also route onward: 'positive responders to a loyalty program or reviews page, and those with concerns to your contact form.' Anonymous by default, 'fully compliant with the GDPR'; contact details only if volunteered, and deleted after 30 days. 37 survey languages. Smiley Link QR codes are tied to a physical terminal, and data merges into one report.
competitors.mobileAnatomy: The phone screen was not observed. Inferred from the brand system and docs: a single question as the headline, then a row of four large faces in fixed colour order from happy to unhappy (dark green, light green, light pink-red, red, as seen in the live logo), then a follow-up chip list, then a text box, then a thank-you. Only three interactions to finish.
competitors.visualStyle: Friendly civic look: four coloured faces as the entire visual language, green brand buttons, rounded sans. Language-free input, but reads as institutional (airports, supermarkets) rather than premium. Their own marketing site (observed) opens with a Cookiebot banner whose primary action is a big green 'Allow all', with no equal 'Reject' button.
competitors.adminBuilder: Surveys hold 'the main question, an optional follow-up question, and optional open feedback'. Several surveys can be scheduled by time of day. Printable QR and URL question sheets are auto-generated from the email report. Smiley Digital comes as Pop-up or Embed scripts with a token and a language variable.
competitors.analytics: HappyOrNot Analytics (19 UI languages): real-time data by time, location and touchpoint; alerts on 'a certain amount of negative feedback'; trend tracking; exports; an AI model over written comments. Vendor claim: Pop-up '80% response rate'.
competitors.compliance: Strong privacy posture (anonymous, GDPR, 30-day deletion of volunteered contact details). Routing positive responders to a reviews page and negative ones to a contact form is gating if the reviews page is a public platform.
standoutIdeas: One question, one tap, language-free faces: the fastest first interaction in the set.
A different question per placement (check-out, bar, spa) matches RepKey's placement-specific welcome copy.
Physical signage formats as a product (table talkers, tents, wobblers, outdoor boards).
Time-of-day scheduling and alerts triggered by a volume of negative feedback.
antiPatterns: Cartoon faces read as cheap for premium hospitality.
Four points with no neutral forces a lean that does not map to Google's 1-5.
A path to the reviews page that only positive responders see.
Cookie-consent dark pattern on the vendor site.

competitors.name: Yelp (Don't Ask for Reviews policy, 'Find us on Yelp' sticker)
competitors.category: Review platform policy and in-venue sticker
competitors.guestFlow: No venue-owned review prompt is allowed. A venue may show a 'Find us on Yelp' window sticker (US/Canada). Guests find the business on Yelp themselves.
competitors.mobileAnatomy: N/A.
competitors.visualStyle: Red Yelp burst sticker; a platform mark, not venue branding.
competitors.adminBuilder: N/A.
competitors.analytics: N/A.
competitors.compliance: Policy observed live: 'Don't ask anyone to review your business'; 'Don't ask for reviews after requesting customer feedback in other places like surveys or contact forms'; 'Your staff should never compete to collect reviews'; no freebies, discounts or payment. Yelp's software may not recommend reviews that look solicited, and a Consumer Alerts pop-up exposes violators. A RepKey portal must never show a 'Review us on Yelp' action after a rating. At most a neutral 'Find us on Yelp' secondary link (low relevance in Bulgaria).
standoutIdeas: 'Find us on' phrasing (discovery rather than solicitation) is useful wording for non-Google platform links in the secondary link tree.
antiPatterns: Any Yelp review ask after a private rating (explicitly prohibited).

competitors.name: Google Business Profile review link and QR (the destination)
competitors.category: Review destination and policy
competitors.guestFlow: The business shares 'a Google link or QR code' that opens the review form. 'Customers must be signed into a Google Account to leave a review.' Everything after the tap happens on Google, so the portal can only know that the guest chose to go there.
competitors.mobileAnatomy: Google's review sheet (not observed): a star row and a text field in Google's UI.
competitors.visualStyle: Google's UI; the venue has no styling control. Google's printable marketing kit (review stickers, table tents) now redirects to google.com/business according to a third-party report, so venues have lost official branded collateral.
competitors.adminBuilder: Business Profile 'Ask for reviews' link or QR (exact steps not captured).
competitors.analytics: None given to the portal; the business sees reviews in its Business Profile.
competitors.compliance: Maps policy text fetched today prohibits: 'Discourage or prohibit negative reviews, or selectively solicit positive reviews from customers'; incentives 'in exchange for posting any review'; merchants who 'require or pressure users to leave ratings or write reviews while on the premises' or request specific content; staff review quotas; and soliciting reviews that name staff (per third-party reports, added April 2026). Allowed: soliciting 'genuine experience, without offering incentives to do so or attempting to influence the rating'. Google removed the explicit gating line in 2021-22 and pointed to its fake-engagement policy; the fetched text contains the selective-solicitation wording again. EU: Omnibus Directive 2019/2161 adds UCPD Annex I 23b ('misrepresenting consumer reviews ... in order to promote products') and 23c, and Art. 7(6) makes 'whether and how the trader ensures that the published reviews originate from consumers' material information.
standoutIdeas: A 'Continue on Google' action with honest copy saying you will need a Google account, and no prefilled or suggested rating or text.
Since Google's branded sticker kit is gone, RepKey can own premium printable table cards per portal.
antiPatterns: Prefilled ratings or suggested review text (it influences the rating).
Asking guests to mention staff by name.

competitors.name: MENU TIGER (QR TIGER)
competitors.category: Digital QR menu and ordering with in-menu one-tap feedback
competitors.guestFlow: Feedback sits inside the QR menu or ordering site: 'Customers rate their experience with a single tap', followed by optional custom questions (Likert, open-ended, ratings) and optional comment boxes. Anonymous by default. 'Customers cannot edit their feedback once it has been submitted.' The feedback page is open to anyone who scans, with no verified-diner option. Surveys are multilingual (19 languages). No Google redirect is documented.
competitors.mobileAnatomy: The guest page was not observed (no public demo store found). The FAQ says the venue's social links 'appear as clickable buttons at the bottom of your website and mobile landing page'.
competitors.visualStyle: The landing page is customisable: 'selecting fonts, colors, images, and layouts to match your restaurant branding'. Template-driven.
competitors.adminBuilder: Menu builder (store, then categories, then items), dynamic QR codes (edit the menu without reprinting), a landing-page theme, and question creation. Average ratings can be displayed publicly or kept private.
competitors.analytics: Real-time notification for every rating; instant alerts on low ratings ('Allow staff to address concerns before customers leave'); feedback by date and location; CSV export; QR scan counts.
competitors.compliance: Markets 'Offer incentives (e.g., discounts) for completed surveys' (the FAQ says to handle it manually outside the system). Publicly showing a self-collected average rating raises EU 23c and Art. 7(6) questions (verification disclosure). Framed as a way to 'Reduce negative online reviews through fast resolution'.
standoutIdeas: A single-tap rating embedded where guests already are (the menu). This supports RepKey showing secondary links like the menu from arrival alongside the rating.
Dynamic QR codes are an owner expectation, which RepKey's stable tokens meet.
antiPatterns: Incentives for feedback (RepKey permanently denies gamification and rewards).
No correction or withdrawal after submission (RepKey allows it, a differentiator).
Public display of a self-collected rating without verification disclosure.

competitors.name: MENU (menu.app, PAR Ordering)
competitors.category: Branded ordering web app with Dynamic Link QR codes
competitors.guestFlow: The QR code opens the store menu, 'potentially with the table number already pre-filled for Table Service'. No guest feedback feature was found. The support page fetch failed on SSL, so this relies on the search engine's summary of the vendor knowledge base.
competitors.mobileAnatomy: Not observed.
competitors.visualStyle: Kiosk, web app and mobile app 'in restaurant branding' (vendor claim).
competitors.adminBuilder: 'Dynamic Links' let brands 'generate static QR codes that can later be reconfigured to direct to a different place in the application while the QR code itself stays the same'.
competitors.analytics: Not captured.
competitors.compliance: N/A.
standoutIdeas: QR codes carrying placement context (table, order type) map to RepKey portal-per-placement with stable tokens.

competitors.name: Linktree (restaurant pages)
competitors.category: Link-in-bio used as a venue link hub on table QR codes
competitors.guestFlow: Instant: the page is the hub, with no rating step. Tapping a button leaves to the menu, booking, map or WhatsApp. No completion state. A cookie banner appeared on first load.
competitors.mobileAnatomy: Riviera Bistro, measured at 375px: a 56px Linktree asterisk badge top-left and a share button top-right; a 96px circular logo (green disc with a cream anchor wordmark) at y=104; H1 'Riviera Bistro' in Link Sans 24px/600, white, at y=213; a 16px/500 descriptor 'Mediterranean Bistro & Bar / Bali, ID. Open 11:30 - LATE'; six full-width black buttons, each 347x64, on a 78px pitch (14px gap), centred 16px/400 white labels with a kebab share icon: Reservations, Website, Menu, Drink List, Location, WhatsApp. The first screen holds exactly the logo, name and six buttons. Below the fold: 'Join rivierabistro on Linktree', Cookie Preferences / Report / Privacy, an 'Explore other Linktrees' carousel of unrelated creators (edsheeran, katseyeworld and others) in 148x192 white 16px-radius cards, and an 'About this account' transparency panel (joined July 2022). Incontro Bistrot: deep teal background; a terracotta logo disc with a column-and-fork mark; the title ends with an Italian flag emoji; tagline 'A tradição Italiana no Porto'; outlined full-pill buttons with left line icons and uppercase labels: MENU, RESERVATIONS, GOOGLE MAPS, WHATSAPP, INSTAGRAM, CONTACTS (with a subline 'Contact · Incontro Caffè Bistrot').
competitors.visualStyle: Venue identity is just a logo disc, one background colour or texture, and one descriptor line. Platform typography (Link Sans). Buttons are either solid dark slabs or outlined pills. Tasteful when the colour is chosen well, but still recognisably 'a Linktree'.
competitors.adminBuilder: Templates and themes; QR code generation for the Linktree URL (Linktree's own blog pitches it for table menus).
competitors.analytics: Per-link click analytics (paid tiers).
competitors.compliance: Cookie banner and third-party platform promotion on a venue's guest page. A 'Rate us on Google' link sitting among the others is not gating, but nothing is recorded.
standoutIdeas: Tall 64px full-width tap targets with icon plus label are the right link-tree ergonomics at phone width.
A one-line descriptor with hours ('Open 11:30 - LATE') gives useful identity without a paragraph.
A no-photo identity (logo disc on a rich solid colour) proves a premium no-image portal is possible.
antiPatterns: The platform cross-promotes other creators below the venue's content.
Cookie banner on a guest page.
A kebab menu on every button adds noise.
Emoji flags in titles; every page looks the same.

competitors.name: Beacons (restaurant link-in-bio)
competitors.category: Creator link-in-bio used by venues
competitors.guestFlow: Instant hub: 'Book a table here', 'See our Menu' (plus meat and salad emoji), 'Rate us on Google' (plus a star emoji), 'Official Website' (plus a globe emoji). The Google review link is just another button, with no private step. A consent or overlay layer had to be dismissed first.
competitors.mobileAnatomy: Food Laboratories at 375px: a full-bleed background photo (café table with a latte, softly blurred) behind everything; a share icon top-right; a large white outlined hexagon logo mark centred at about 180-370px; H1 'Food Laboratories' in a bold geometric sans (Poppins-like) at roughly 30px, white; TikTok and Instagram icons; then stacked frosted cream pill buttons (about 400x90 at 0.6 scale, green 2px border, dark grey semibold labels with text-shadow). The fourth button is below the fold.
competitors.visualStyle: Photo-as-wallpaper with glassy buttons: atmospheric, but label contrast on frosted glass over a busy photo is weak, and emoji do the iconography.
competitors.adminBuilder: Links Block where each link 'can be individually scheduled, animated, and tracked'.
competitors.analytics: Per-link click analytics.
competitors.compliance: 'Rate us on Google' as an ungated link is compliant, but no private channel exists.
standoutIdeas: Scheduling links (for example a brunch menu only on weekends) is a useful idea for RepKey secondary link categories later.
antiPatterns: Low-contrast labels over a photo background.
Emoji as UI.
A review button styled the same as the menu button, with no hierarchy.

competitors.name: Tap Bio and Koji (defunct or closing link-in-bio)
competitors.category: Link-in-bio platforms
competitors.guestFlow: Tap Bio: 'Instead of a single long page with a list of links, it creates swipeable cards' (six card types: links, images, text, video, X posts, email capture). Koji: interactive mini-app widgets in bio pages.
competitors.mobileAnatomy: Tap Bio: horizontally swipeable full-screen cards, one topic per card (not observed; tap.bio navigation was blocked).
competitors.visualStyle: Card-per-topic, background and button colour customisation only.
competitors.adminBuilder: N/A.
competitors.analytics: N/A.
competitors.compliance: N/A.
standoutIdeas: Lesson for the sales story: Koji shut down on 31 Jan 2024 after Linktree bought it, and Tap Bio announced shutdown for 31 Oct 2026 ('Users lose login access, and Tap Bio removes all pages'). Printed table QR codes that point at third-party link-in-bio pages die with the platform. RepKey's stable tokens tied to the property are a durability argument owners understand.
antiPatterns: Swipe-card navigation hides links behind gestures, which is poor for a quick in-venue task.

crossCuttingPatterns: First-interaction speed has two fast archetypes. (a) One question with a language-free scale as the first thing on screen (HappyOrNot: one question, four faces, done in three taps; sunday and me&u: a star row straight after payment). (b) A link hub with zero steps (Linktree, Beacons: the first screen is logo, name and 4-6 buttons). The Ratestar reference does neither: a hero video, contacts, social icons and a paragraph all come before any action. For RepKey, keep the private star row inside the first 812px screen, and let a compact link row sit below it from arrival.

Rating inputs seen: 5 stars (sunday, me&u, OpenTable, Resy, Toast handheld), thumbs (Toast receipts, Toast Pay per dish), 4 faces with no neutral (HappyOrNot), out of 10 (TheFork), one-tap or Likert (MENU TIGER). Stars dominate wherever the next step is Google. That is also a risk, because guests can mistake private stars for the Google rating (sunday even prefills Google with them). RepKey should label the row visibly as private to the venue and never carry the score over to Google.

Review gating is the default in restaurant tools, not the exception. me&u (configurable minimum star rating, on by default), sunday (satisfied guests get a Google button, dissatisfied ones a private channel), Tablein ('If the review is very high' the guest is invited to Google, Tripadvisor or Facebook), and HappyOrNot Smiley Sign (positive responders to a reviews page, concerns to a contact form). Only the tools that never route to Google avoid it (OpenTable, Resy, Toast Pay). Rules they conflict with: Google Maps policy ('selectively solicit positive reviews'; no pressure 'while on the premises'; no incentives), Tripadvisor ('the user interface and experience for submitting positive and negative reviews must be identical'), Yelp (don't ask at all, and not after a survey), and EU UCPD Annex I 23b/23c plus Art. 7(6). RepKey's 'Google for every guest' plus 'private feedback additionally at or below the threshold' is a real, sellable differentiator: pitch it to owners as the version that cannot get their profile flagged.

OpenTable's form is the best compliant pattern: the public review and a 'confidential note to the restaurant' sit in one flow that is the same for every score. In RepKey terms, after rating show the same Google action at the same size and position for every score, and show private feedback as an added option below it, never as a replacement or a detour.

Venue identity in these tools uses at most three levers: a logo disc or wordmark, one background or accent colour (Riviera: olive-black; Incontro: deep teal and terracotta; me&u Market House: burgundy rgb(93,9,35) on white), and one photo (me&u header 375x131, Beacons wallpaper). Add a one-line voice descriptor ('Open 11:30 - LATE', 'A tradição Italiana no Porto', 'Dogs welcome, people can come too'). Typography almost never belongs to the venue (Link Sans, Manrope, Poppins). Curated type pairings per property would immediately look more premium than every restaurant tool in this set, and would carry the no-photo requirement.

Link-hub ergonomics converge on full-width stacked buttons 56-64px tall with 12-16px gaps, a centred or icon-left label, and Menu or Reservations first, then Website, Maps or Location, then WhatsApp or Instagram. None of the observed tools groups links into categories. Emoji often stand in for icons (Beacons, Ratestar). RepKey's ordered categories can use real line icons and short secondary lines (for example 'Menu · Today until 23:00').

Post-rating and thank-you states in payment flows stack tip, rating, Google or feedback, loyalty and thank-you. The one element that feels premium is the venue-voice closing line (sunday: 'It was a pleasure cooking for you tonight! You're always welcome here.'). For RepKey the completion state should be a warm venue-authored sentence, the same Google action, and a quiet receipt area (correct, withdraw, reset device), with no promos or perks.

Low-rating handling across the set: instant staff alerts (Toast SMS with 'negative only' / 'all' / 'none' presets; MENU TIGER; HappyOrNot volume-based alerts; me&u Crew 'Fast Feedback' so staff can fix it in-venue); a morning digest (Resy, sunday); a weekly email (Toast Menu Item Review, Thursdays); AI theme summaries (Toast: 'Atmosphere, Service, Food Quality, Wait Time'; sunday: Food & Drink, Service Quality, Ambiance, Value for Money); context on each item (table, server, seated time). For RepKey's admin phase: notify responsible managers at or below the threshold, digest by Portal and Portal Group, and use the portal or placement as the context field.

Privacy stance: HappyOrNot anonymous by default with volunteered contacts deleted after 30 days; MENU TIGER anonymous but no editing; Toast Pay passes no contact details; OpenTable hides diner email from restaurants. Meanwhile the link-in-bio pages (Linktree, Beacons) and HappyOrNot's own site open with cookie banners (HappyOrNot's primary button is 'Allow all'). A guest portal with no cookie banner and a one-line 'Private to [venue]. No account, no tracking.' is itself a visible premium signal.

What makes owners proud to put the QR on the table: (1) their own brand, not the vendor's, above the fold (logo, colour, photo); (2) physical collateral that matches the interior (vendors sell acrylic, laser-etched wood table stands and table tents; HappyOrNot sells table talkers, tents, wobblers and outdoor boards; Google's review sticker kit is reportedly retired); (3) visible results (sunday sells 'G 4.9 · +350 5 on Google' charts). RepKey opportunity: premium printable table cards per portal with a stable token, and an admin analytics hero built on qualified_scans, portal_rating_count and portal_rating_average. Never claim Google reviews were written, only 'guests who chose Google'.

Stable QR codes are table stakes: Menu.app Dynamic Links and MENU TIGER dynamic QR let owners change content without reprinting. The deaths of link-in-bio platforms (Koji, Feb 2024; Tap Bio, 31 Oct 2026) show that printed codes pointing at a third-party hub are fragile. RepKey's stable QR/NFC tokens plus draft/publish/rollback answer both concerns.

Language handling is weakly documented across restaurant tools: HappyOrNot has 37 survey languages; MENU TIGER has 19 languages with manual menu translation; me&u advertises translations; Linktree and Beacons have none (single-language owner copy). A visible EN/BG switch with fully reviewed copy would stand out in the Bulgarian market.
surprises: sunday's help centre says guests are redirected to Google 'with the rating already prefilled'. This is a vendor claim; Google documents no official prefill, so the method is inferred to be unofficial. Its own blog says Google prohibits review gating, while its post-payment article describes a Google button for satisfied guests only.

me&u documents threshold gating in plain language ('Configure the minimum star rating for which you would like guests to be prompted to leave a Google review'), and the whole feedback feature is a 'beta feature' switched on by default.
HappyOrNot, known for anonymous neutral smileys, markets Smiley Sign as routing 'positive responders to a loyalty program or reviews page, and those with concerns to your contact form'.

Google removed the explicit anti-gating line from its Maps policy in 2021-22 (reported by Search Engine Roundtable), but the policy text fetched now again prohibits 'selectively solicit positive reviews'. Third-party reports say an April 2026 update also bans staff review quotas and soliciting reviews that name staff.
Toast Pay's dish review never mentions Google and deliberately shows the most expensive items first (up to three).
MENU TIGER openly suggests discounts for completed surveys and lets venues show their self-collected average rating in public.
Linktree venue pages end with an 'Explore other Linktrees' carousel promoting Ed Sheeran and other creators directly under a restaurant's links.
Tap Bio is shutting down on 31 Oct 2026 and Koji died in Feb 2024: printed table QR codes pointing at link-in-bio pages break with the platform.

Google's printable marketing kit ('Review us on Google' stickers and table tents) reportedly now redirects to google.com/business (third-party report), leaving venues without official branded review collateral.
OpenTable's photo rules reject pictures that show people (including staff), menus, or plates of food already eaten.

Salvage caveat: the earlier agent's WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200). The TheFork live review page, the tap.bio home page, the Toast receipts blog and the HappyOrNot language subdomain all failed to load. No guest review screen of sunday, me&u or Toast was observed live, because each requires a real transaction.

patterns.name: 1. Ask one overall question first, with no category sub-scores
patterns.examples: Airbnb asks for an overall 1–5 star rating that is independent of its six category ratings; the listing average uses the overall score only ([Hostfully summary](https://www.hostfully.com/blog/airbnb-review-policy/), [Airbnb help](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/13)). Booking.com makes the overall 1–10 score the one required input. Its sub-scores are optional and do not affect the score, and it had to add an alert when sub-scores and the overall score disagree by more than 5 points ([The Reputation Lab](https://www.thereputationlab.com/what-you-need-to-know-about-recent-changes-in-booking-com-s-scoring-system/)). In Google Maps the first step is tapping one of 5 empty stars; the text is optional ([Google Maps help](https://support.google.com/maps/answer/6230175?hl=en&co=GENIE.Platform%3DAndroid)). GOV.UK recommends one question per page ([GOV.UK question pages](https://design-system.service.gov.uk/patterns/question-pages/)). Typeform and Tally are built around showing one question at a time ([Tally settings](https://tally.so/help/form-settings)).
patterns.whyItWorks: The guest faces one decision with low effort and nothing to compare. The overall score is the signal every platform actually aggregates. Adding sub-scores creates inconsistent answers and extra decisions, and Booking.com needed a guard against exactly that.
patterns.fitForRepKey: This matches the product: `portal_rating_count` and `portal_rating_average` are single overall values. On arrival, show the question, 5 stars and one submit action. Leave categories and tags out of the beta. Everything else (Google, private note, links) comes after the rating or sits below the rating block.
patterns.risks: Owners will ask for category ratings (cleanliness, staff). Treat that as a separate product decision with its own data model. Do not add it as decoration in a design.

patterns.name: 2. Empty outline stars, filled up to the selection, with state shown by contrast and not only by hue
patterns.examples: Google Maps presents 5 empty stars. The W3C APG rating radio group draws stars with `currentcolor` strokes so they survive Windows High Contrast / forced colours, and uses a 2px focus ring with spacing ([APG rating example](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/radio/examples/radio-rating/)). The WCAG 1.4.11 Understanding page uses star ratings as its example. A yellow-versus-white hue change alone fails. A solid fill with contrast, or a thicker border plus fill, passes, and the unselected boundary itself needs 3:1 ([Understanding 1.4.11](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/non-text-contrast.html)).
patterns.whyItWorks: Filling every star up to the chosen one is the familiar model: 4 means four filled stars. Outlines tell the guest the stars are tappable before any interaction. A change in fill and stroke weight is visible to colour-blind users and in forced-colours mode.
patterns.fitForRepKey: **Current gap (verified in `src/components/features/guest/public-portal/guest-response-fields.tsx`):** `RatingChoices` draws the same ★ glyph in five bordered boxes. It has no checked-state styling, so the only visual response to a selection is a focus ring. The redesign should use outline stars at 3:1 or more against the surface, a solid filled star plus a heavier stroke for 1..n, and a single accent. Measured examples: a champagne outline (#C8B48A) on ink (#111418) is 9.1:1 and passes. The same champagne on ivory (#F6F1E7) is only 1.8:1 and fails, so a light theme needs a darker bronze (#8A6D3B on ivory is 4.31:1). A 'dimmed' grey outline (#5C6168) on ink is 2.96:1, a common near-miss.
patterns.risks: Metallic gradients inside the star shapes can drop below 3:1 at their lightest stop. Always measure the flat equivalent. Half-stars do not belong in an input.

patterns.name: 3. Word labels at both ends of the scale, plus a live caption for the chosen value
patterns.examples: NN/g recommends labelled scales with clear opposite endpoints ([NN/g rating scales](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/rating-scales/)). Typeform lets authors label the ends of a rating question. Qualtrics ships NPS with two default endpoint labels and recommends keeping them ([Qualtrics NPS](https://www.qualtrics.com/support/survey-platform/survey-module/editing-questions/question-types-guide/specialty-questions/net-promoter-score/)). Booking.com maps its numbers to word bands. Amazon labels each star (1 = hate … 5 = love).
patterns.whyItWorks: Guests do not share one meaning for '3 stars'. A word removes the doubt. A caption that updates on selection ('4 · Very good') confirms the choice without a dialog.
patterns.fitForRepKey: Put a quiet small-caps label under stars 1 and 5 (EN 'Poor' / 'Excellent'; BG 'Слабо' / 'Отлично' — final copy needs a native speaker) and a fixed-height caption line that shows the chosen value's word. The accessible name of each radio should start with its number and include the word ('4 stars, Very good'), to satisfy 2.5.3 Label in Name ([Understanding 2.5.3](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/label-in-name.html)). Use neutral quality words rather than Amazon's emotional wording, so no score reads as 'right'. This also fixes Signature Stay, which shows the digits 1–5 with no words.
patterns.risks: Bulgarian words run longer, so give the caption a reserved line height to avoid layout shift. If there are digits, labels and a caption all at once, the star row gets cluttered. Choose words over digits.

patterns.name: 4. Selecting a star never submits: one explicit, always-enabled submit
patterns.examples: WCAG technique F36 names auto-submitting a form when the last field changes as a failure. It recommends normal submit-button behaviour ([W3C F36](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG20/Techniques/failures/F36)). Tally's auto-jump moves to the next page after a rating but never submits; the final page needs a manual Submit ([Tally](https://tally.so/help/form-settings)). Apple's in-app rating prompt: tap a star, then Submit ([iMore](https://www.imore.com/how-use-and-turn-app-ratings-and-reviews)). Sheri Byrne-Haber argues for a submit button that stays active and validates on press rather than a disabled one ([article](https://www.sheribyrnehaber.com/accessibility-and-usability-inline-field-validation-vs-constantly-active-submit-button/)).
patterns.whyItWorks: In a native radio group the arrow keys change the checked value on every press. Auto-submitting would record in-between values for keyboard and screen-reader users. On touch it would also lock in a mis-tap from a wobbly thumb.
patterns.fitForRepKey: Keep the existing explicit submit and on-submit validation (`GuestRatingForm` already shows `copy.chooseRating` in a `role=alert`). Put the button directly under the stars. Make its label say privacy, e.g. 'Send privately' / 'Изпрати поверително', rather than Signature Stay's 'Share my rating', which suggests posting publicly. Because the response is real and counted by the analytics, commit-on-tap plus undo was considered and rejected.
patterns.risks: One extra tap. Reduce the cost by making the button visibly respond when a star is chosen (the caption appears, the button gets full emphasis) instead of enabling a disabled button.

patterns.name: 5. Large, centred, evenly spaced targets
patterns.examples: WCAG 2.2 SC 2.5.8 requires at least 24×24 CSS px, or a 24px circle of spacing that does not overlap another target ([Understanding 2.5.8](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/target-size-minimum.html)). Apple's HIG asks for at least 44×44pt and Material 3 for 48×48dp ([LogRocket summary](https://blog.logrocket.com/ux-design/all-accessible-touch-target-sizes/)). Hoober's touch research found people tap the centre of the screen more accurately and more confidently than the edges. It suggests about 11–12mm targets near the edges and as small as 7mm in the centre ([Smashing cheatsheet](https://www.smashingmagazine.com/2023/04/accessible-tap-target-sizes-rage-taps-clicks/), [UXmatters](https://www.uxmatters.com/mt/archives/2017/07/design-for-fingers-touch-and-people-part-3.php)).
patterns.whyItWorks: The stars are the single most important control. Big targets in the middle of the screen, where tapping is most accurate, cut mis-taps. Mis-taps matter more here because Booking.com-style inconsistency guards are not planned.
patterns.fitForRepKey: Hit areas of 56×56px with 12px gaps take 328px, which fits the 358px content width at 390px with 16px gutters. At 320px, use 52px targets with 7px gaps (288px). Draw the star at 32–36px inside the hit area, and make the whole label tappable. Centre the row horizontally. The submit button should be at least 48px tall.
patterns.risks: Decorative spacing that shrinks the hit areas. Star glyphs placed edge to edge with no gaps, which invites mis-taps between neighbours.

patterns.name: 6. The first screen answers where am I, what is asked and how private it is, with no wall in front
patterns.examples: NN/g's QR guidelines call for context, mobile-friendly destinations and deep links straight to the relevant action ([NN/g QR guidelines](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/qr-code-guidelines/)). Google Search Central treats full-page interstitials, including app-install prompts, as intrusive, and prefers small dismissible banners ([Google Search Central](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/avoid-intrusive-interstitials)). Hoober found 49% of people use a one-handed grip and that grips change often ([UXmatters](https://www.uxmatters.com/mt/archives/2013/02/how-do-users-really-hold-mobile-devices.php)). In the Ratestar reference, the photo hero fills about 55% of the first screen and the first action starts at roughly two-thirds of the height.
patterns.whyItWorks: The guest has just scanned a card and has only a few seconds of attention. Seeing the property name confirms they landed in the right place. With the question and stars in the reachable lower-middle band, one thumb is enough.
patterns.fitForRepKey: Composition from top to bottom: an identity strip (wordmark or monogram, plus a small placement line such as 'Reception'). Language switch at top-right. Then the question, stars, caption, submit and a one-line privacy note. The rating block must fit inside the small viewport (`svh`) at 375×667 with the Safari toolbars showing. Use `svh`/`dvh`, not `100vh` ([web.dev viewport units](https://web.dev/blog/viewport-units)), and `env(safe-area-inset-bottom)`. RepKey sets no trackers and no cookies, so the page needs no consent banner. That is a real premium advantage; keep it. No splash screen, intro animation, app prompt or language modal.
patterns.risks: A tall hero, whether photo or type-only, can push the stars below the fold. In iOS 26 Safari, fixed or sticky elements near the bottom edge set the toolbar tint, so a sticky CTA bar can conflict with it ([Jahir Fiquitiva](https://jahir.dev/blog/safari-toolbar), [Ben Frain](https://benfrain.com/ios26-safari-theme-color-tab-tinting-with-fixed-position-elements/)). Prefer an in-flow button to a fixed bottom bar.

patterns.name: 7. State privacy where the guest acts, in guest language
patterns.examples: Airbnb keeps two channels apart: a private note seen only by the host, and a public review ([Airbnb help](https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/13)). Uber tells riders that drivers never see the individual rating ([Uber help](https://help.uber.com/riders/article/rating-a-driver?nodeId=478d7463-99cb-48ff-a81f-0ab227a1e267)). Signature Stay put the line 'Shared privately with Avela Resort' under the button, which is the right place.
patterns.whyItWorks: Guests are more candid when they know who will read the answer. A privacy claim works best right next to the action, not in a policy link.
patterns.fitForRepKey: Under the submit button: 'Only the {Property} team sees your rating' plus the privacy link. Do not describe internal rules (thresholds, eligibility), which the prior README flagged. After submission, the receipt repeats the word 'privately'.
patterns.risks: Over-reassurance reads as nervous. Keep it to one line, and never promise anonymity in stronger terms than the system can guarantee.

patterns.name: 8. Offer the same Google invitation after every score (no gating)
patterns.examples: Google's Maps content policy forbids merchants from discouraging negative reviews or asking to "selectively solicit positive reviews". It also forbids pressuring on-premises reviews and incentives ([Google Maps UGC policy](https://support.google.com/contributionpolicy/answer/7400114)). The FTC says asking only customers you think are happy is not banned by its Rule but could violate the FTC Act ([FTC Q&A](https://www.ftc.gov/business-guidance/resources/consumer-reviews-testimonials-rule-questions-answers)). Bulgaria's Omnibus implementation requires traders to disclose how reviews are obtained and checked ([Mondaq](https://www.mondaq.com/dodd-frank-consumer-protection-act/1199876/bulgaria-implemented-the-omnibus-directive-more-transparency-or-yet-another-burden-for-compliance)). Counter-examples of score-dependent follow-ups: Bolt offers tipping only after 4–5 stars ([Bolt](https://bolt.eu/en/support/articles/360014247060/)), and Uber offers compliments only after 5 stars.
patterns.whyItWorks: Identical treatment is the only design that is plainly not gating. It also removes the suspicion that the page is steering the guest.
patterns.fitForRepKey: After any rating from 1 to 5, the Google card has the same copy, position, size, colour, icon and entrance motion. For ratings at or below the threshold, the private-feedback offer goes below the Google card and adds to it: it never replaces, pushes down, collapses or restyles the Google card. Do not put five filled stars on the Google card, as Ratestar does, because that shows an expected score. Use Google's name and a neutral invitation instead ('Share your experience on Google'). No urgency, no 'please give us 5 stars', no mention of staff by name.
patterns.risks: Copy drift per score (e.g. 'We'd love your 5-star review!' shown only to happy guests) quietly becomes gating. Treat the Google card as one component with no score-dependent props.

patterns.name: 9. The hand-off to Google is honest: record the click, never claim a review
patterns.examples: Google's review link/QR opens Google's own review form ([Google Business Profile help](https://support.google.com/business/answer/16816815?hl=en)). Posting needs a Google sign-in, and the text is optional ([Google Maps help](https://support.google.com/maps/answer/6230175?hl=en&co=GENIE.Platform%3DAndroid)).
patterns.whyItWorks: If the guest knows they are leaving the page and that Google may ask them to sign in, the sign-in screen is not a surprise. A truthful state when they return keeps trust.
patterns.fitForRepKey: Put a small note on the card: 'Opens Google · you may need to sign in'. Mark the external link with an arrow icon and screen-reader text. When the guest comes back, show 'Google opened' or simply the unchanged receipt. Never show 'Thanks for your review' (RepKey can only observe the selection). If the destination is stale, replace the card with gentle copy such as 'Public reviews are not available right now — your private rating reached the team' and render no link at all.
patterns.risks: On Android the link may open inside the Maps app and never return to the browser tab. Do not build the flow on the assumption that the guest comes back.

patterns.name: 10. Private written feedback is an extra step for low scores and never a detour
patterns.examples: Uber asks for issue feedback on ratings below 5 ([Uber help](https://help.uber.com/riders/article/rating-a-driver?nodeId=478d7463-99cb-48ff-a81f-0ab227a1e267)). Airbnb offers lists of what went well and what could have gone better. NN/g recommends an optional free-text 'why' after a rating ([NN/g](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/rating-scales/)).
patterns.whyItWorks: It catches a service recovery chance while the guest is still in the moment, and it asks for nothing more than the score from guests who do not want to write.
patterns.fitForRepKey: At or below the threshold, show a card after the Google card: 'Tell the team privately what could be better' → a textarea opens in place, with its own 'Send privately' button. Asking for names or contact details is blocked, so the placeholder must not invite personal data ('No need to include your name'). Quick-pick chips ('Room', 'Service'…) would be a new data model: mark them future scope. Never add Uber-style compliment badges; they are gamification.
patterns.risks: If the private card is visually louder than the Google card, it reads as demoting Google. Give the two the same visual weight, or make the private card slightly quieter.

patterns.name: 11. Show an inline receipt with Change and Withdraw instead of confirmation dialogs
patterns.examples: NN/g warns that too many confirmation dialogs get ignored and favours undo ([NN/g confirmation dialogs](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/confirmation-dialog/), [User control and freedom](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/user-control-and-freedom/)). Google Maps lets people edit or delete a review later. Bolt ratings cannot be changed after submission, which is the anti-pattern ([Bolt](https://bolt.eu/en/support/articles/115002918034/)).
patterns.whyItWorks: Guests can commit quickly without anxiety because the path to change their answer is visible.
patterns.fitForRepKey: After saving, the star row collapses into a single line: '★★★★☆ 4 · Very good — sent privately · Change'. Correction, withdrawal and 'Using a shared device? Clear this response' go in a quiet 'Your response' disclosure at the bottom, so they are available without making the page look like a console. The withdraw copy must say it does not affect anything already posted on Google.
patterns.risks: Hiding the rights too well. The disclosure needs a clear label and must be reachable by keyboard.

patterns.name: 12. Saving, error and completion states that never lose input or steal focus
patterns.examples: WCAG 4.1.3 requires status messages that assistive technology announces without moving focus, using `role=status` for success and alert for errors ([Understanding 4.1.3](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/status-messages.html)). NN/g's peak-end rule says endings and failures stay in memory the longest ([NN/g peak-end](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/peak-end-rule/)). Hotel captive portals and congested guest wifi are a known source of slow and failed requests ([Purple](https://www.purple.ai/en-us/guides/diagnosing-guest-wifi-network-congestion)).
patterns.whyItWorks: On hotel wifi, failed requests are common. A calm retry that keeps the chosen star turns a failure into a small bump instead of the lasting memory of the visit.
patterns.fitForRepKey: The button label changes to 'Sending…' and keeps its width. On failure, the selection stays, an inline message explains the problem ('Couldn't send — check your connection and try again'), and a Retry button appears. On success: `role=status` 'Rating sent privately'. When the form is replaced by the after-rating view, move focus to that view's heading (`tabindex=-1`) so keyboard and screen-reader users do not land on `<body>`. The ending is a quiet thank-you plus modest next actions, not a sales push.
patterns.risks: Double submission during a slow request. Keep the existing pending-disable and idempotent server behaviour.

patterns.name: 13. Native radio semantics, keyboard and focus details
patterns.examples: APG radio and rating radio group: Tab goes to the checked radio (or the first one), arrow keys move and check, and a roving tabindex is used ([APG radio pattern](https://www.w3.org/WAI/ARIA/apg/patterns/radio/)). Atomic A11y checklist: fieldset and legend for the name, and a state announcement for each option ([atomica11y](https://www.atomica11y.com/accessible-web/star-rating/)). Graham's no-JS radio star rating shows why inputs must be visually hidden rather than set to `display:none` ([DEV](https://dev.to/grahamthedev/5-star-rating-system-actually-accessible-no-js-no-wai-aria-3idl)). WCAG 2.4.11 requires that focus is not fully hidden under sticky elements ([Understanding 2.4.11](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/focus-not-obscured-minimum.html)).
patterns.whyItWorks: Native radios give correct announcements for free ('4 stars, Very good, radio button, checked, 4 of 5') and work before or without JavaScript.
patterns.fitForRepKey: Keep the current native inputs in `<fieldset>`/`<legend>`. The explicit `role=radiogroup` plus an `aria-label` that repeats the legend can make screen readers announce the group name twice; test it and drop it if so. Hide the inputs with a clip-style `sr-only` (already done). The focus ring should be 2px with a 2px offset, at least 3:1 against both the surface and the star. Use `currentColor` strokes for forced-colours mode. Set `scroll-padding` if anything is sticky.
patterns.risks: Custom div/button 'stars' without radio semantics. Hover-preview fill on touch devices, which can get stuck in the hovered state.

patterns.name: 14. Detect the language, keep a visible switch labelled with native names, never use flags
patterns.examples: W3C advises serving the language from Accept-Language while keeping a visible link to the other languages on every page. It also advises remembering an explicit choice, not using flags, and naming each language in itself ([W3C i18n](https://www.w3.org/International/questions/qa-site-conneg)). The Ratestar reference uses a UK flag dropdown. WP29 Opinion 04/2012 treats a user-chosen language preference as consent-exempt interface customisation ([EDRi summary](https://edri.org/our-work/edrigramnumber10-12article29-wp-cookie-exemption/)).
patterns.whyItWorks: Most guests land in the right language without doing anything. Anyone the detection got wrong can switch with one tap, and flags do not misrepresent languages.
patterns.fitForRepKey: `PortalLanguageNav` already uses 'Български' / 'English' text links with `hreflang`, `aria-current` and a `?locale=` URL. That fits the no-cookie posture; keep it and restyle it as a quiet two-item control at top-right, 44px or more tall. Add `lang` on each link and set `<html lang>` per locale. That lang attribute is also what switches on Bulgarian Cyrillic letter forms (see type notes).
patterns.risks: Auto-redirecting based on IP. A compact 'EN | БГ' is fine visually, but the accessible name must be the full language name.

patterns.name: 15. A performance budget built for congested hotel wifi and in-app QR browsers
patterns.examples: web.dev Core Web Vitals targets at the 75th percentile: LCP within 2.5s, INP within 200ms ([web.dev vitals](https://web.dev/articles/vitals)). web.dev on preloading: preload only resources the browser discovers late; too many preloads hurt on slow networks; preloaded fonts need `crossorigin` ([web.dev preload](https://web.dev/articles/preload-critical-assets)). web.dev font guidance: WOFF2 only, `unicode-range` subsets, `swap` versus `optional`, and `size-adjust` fallbacks against layout shift ([web.dev fonts](https://web.dev/articles/font-best-practices)). A wifi vendor suggests keeping splash pages around 500KB ([Fydelia](https://www.fydelia.com/blog/trending-question-why-do-guest-wifi-splash-pages-load-so-slowly-and-how-to-fix-it)). QR-menu guidance: test from every seat on a slow network and never send guests to a PDF ([Ogent](https://restaurant.ogent.ai/qr-code-menu-best-practices-for-restaurants/)).
patterns.whyItWorks: The first paint decides whether the guest waits. Hero video, three font families and a photo carousel, as in the Ratestar reference, cost seconds on a shared hotel link.
patterns.fitForRepKey: No-photo variant: under about 150KB total transfer. At most 2 WOFF2 files (the display face used for the question, which is the LCP element and is the only preload, plus one text face), subset to Latin and Cyrillic. Grain as a tiny tiled image or a CSS data-URI, not a live SVG filter. No autoplay video in the beta. If a historical `hero_image_url` renders, give it an explicit size, AVIF/WebP, `fetchpriority=high` only when it is the LCP element, and a solid-colour placeholder behind it.
patterns.risks: Tenant logos from organisation uploads have no size limit. Resize them or give them explicit dimensions. Serving the display font late turns into a visible reflow of the headline.

patterns.name: 16. Light and dark polarity is a brand choice made with contrast and night use in mind
patterns.examples: NN/g reports that dark text on a light background reads better for people with normal vision, even under night-time conditions, and that the advantage grows as text gets smaller. It recommends supporting both modes ([NN/g dark mode](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/dark-mode/)). NN/g's QR guidelines say printed codes should be dark on light for reliable scanning ([NN/g QR](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/qr-code-guidelines/)). iOS 26 Safari derives its toolbar tint from the page background ([Jahir Fiquitiva](https://jahir.dev/blog/safari-toolbar)).
patterns.whyItWorks: A dark ink page feels premium and gentle in a dark room, but small, thin text on dark backgrounds is harder to read. The fix is size and weight, not abandoning dark.
patterns.fitForRepKey: Signature Stay can stay dark, with body text at 17–18px, weights of 400 or more, text at 7:1 or more and no hairline serifs below about 20px. Every direction needs a light variant (the admin picks one; following `prefers-color-scheme` is optional). Give `body` an explicit background so Safari tints correctly. Printed QR material stays dark on light whatever the page theme.
patterns.risks: Pure black with pure white text causes halation. Use a softened ink such as #111418 with warm off-white text (#D9D2C3 on it measures 12.3:1).

patterns.name: 17. No emoji in the interface, and only a few icons
patterns.examples: Léonie Watson shows emoji are announced unreliably, or only by their Unicode names, unless they are exposed deliberately ([tink.uk](https://tink.uk/accessible-emoji/)). The W3C note on decorative Unicode characters recommends `aria-hidden` ([W3C wiki](https://www.w3.org/WAI/GL/wiki/Using_a_Decorative_Unicode_Character)). The Ratestar reference uses 📍, ☎ and ⚜ as UI.
patterns.whyItWorks: Emoji render differently on each operating system, undercut a premium look and add noise to screen-reader output.
patterns.fitForRepKey: Use text first ('Velingrad · Rhodope Mountains') and 1.5px-stroke SVG icons marked `aria-hidden` next to real text. The ★ glyph in the current fields should become an SVG star, which gives control over stroke contrast.
patterns.risks: Mixing icon sets. Use one stroke weight and one corner style.

patterns.name: 18. Secondary links as quiet rows below the rating
patterns.examples: Signature Stay draws links as hairline rows with an arrow. Feed's Hoxton redesign used minimal tones and simple transitions and did not over-brand ([Feed](https://www.feed.xyz/project/thehoxton)). The Ratestar reference uses full-width photo cards, which compete with the review action.
patterns.whyItWorks: A link tree that sits below the rating reads as a service, not a distraction, so the page still leads with the rating.
patterns.fitForRepKey: This supports the proposed 'links from arrival' change without breaking the rule that the rating comes first. Put the rows under the rating block after a hairline and a small heading ('Also useful' / 'Полезно'). Rows are 52px or taller, with the label left, the destination type in small text and an arrow right. No photos, no counts, no badges.
patterns.risks: Owners add eight links. Recommend no more than 4 visible and group the rest by category.

aesthetics.whatToTake: Restraint as the luxury signal. Construct's identity draws on early alphabets and carved marks, with flared terminals, a light line weight, and earthy sand, soil and clay tones. It lives on uncoated papers with embossing and gold foil ([BP&O](https://bpando.org/2016/02/16/branding-aman/)). Online it has almost no interface chrome: editorial serif headings and small-caps labels between full-bleed photographs. For RepKey, the no-photo version of this is a flared-terminal serif question, small-caps place lines, wide margins and a single warm metal accent.
aesthetics.whatToAvoid: Copying Aman's photo-led page rhythm, because photography is blocked in the beta. Also avoid thin weights on dark backgrounds, which fail at small sizes.

aesthetics.whatToTake: A proven no-photo device from inside the Aman family: abstract, hand-dyed-looking gradients with one signature accent colour per destination, beside a chiselled wordmark ([Hingston](https://www.hingston.studio/work/janu-by-aman/)). For RepKey this suggests a property-tinted gradient field with grain behind the identity strip, which can be tuned per property without uploads.
aesthetics.whatToAvoid: Rainbow or neon gradients that read as a tech startup. Keep to 2–3 related hues at low chroma.

aesthetics.whatToTake: A clear pairing strategy: all-caps Canto for display next to Avenir Next Condensed for web text, and a six-dot brush mark taken from Thai blessing marks ([Fonts In Use](https://fontsinuse.com/uses/36800/six-senses)). Lesson: one characterful display face plus a narrow, efficient text face that saves width for Bulgarian.
aesthetics.whatToAvoid: Condensed text at small sizes on dark backgrounds, and borrowing culturally specific marks.

aesthetics.reference: Ace Hotel (Atelier Ace; Sydney signage by Studio Ongarato)
aesthetics.whatToTake: Local craft as identity. The Sydney signage uses a custom geometric typeface cut into timber and ceramic, with deep carving that plays light against shadow ([Studio Ongarato](https://studioongarato.com.au/journal/collaboration-craft-for-ace-hotel/)). For RepKey: a type-only portal can feel made for the place through a place line, a local material texture (stone, timber grain) as a subtle surface, and a custom-feeling wordmark.
aesthetics.whatToAvoid: Imitating fake handmade texture with heavy bitmaps. Keep textures tiny and tiled.

aesthetics.whatToTake: Mobile-first. Each hotel gets a palette curated from its location photography and illustrations by local artists, while simple transitions and minimal tones keep the whole group consistent ([Feed](https://www.feed.xyz/project/thehoxton)). For RepKey: one system with per-property palette tokens, which suits groups of properties.
aesthetics.whatToAvoid: A magazine-like density of modules. A rating page needs one focus.

aesthetics.whatToTake: Personality through voice. The verbal identity is witty and worldly without being condescending; the doormat that says 'nice shoes' is the famous example ([The Subtext](https://www.thesubtext.online/all/citizenm-verbal-identity), [KesselsKramer](https://www.kesselskramer.com/project/citizenm-hotel)). For RepKey: let the property's welcome line carry warmth, and keep the chrome text plain.
aesthetics.whatToAvoid: Jokes around the rating and the Google action. Humour near a score can read as pressure or as mocking a low rating.

aesthetics.whatToTake: A monochrome, deliberately neutral system that lets the members do the talking. It combines a serif display face with a grotesk and a grid derived from its 3×3 icon ([KOVA](https://www.kovacollective.co/post/soho-house-a-case-study-on-branding-going-beyond-the-visuals), [PLUS](https://www.plusagency.co.uk/case-study/soho-house-redefining-their-brand-identity/)). For RepKey: the RepKey chrome stays neutral so the property's own identity is the loud part.
aesthetics.whatToAvoid: Club-style exclusivity copy. Guests are not members.

aesthetics.whatToTake: Black-and-white monochrome collateral carrying a suminagashi ink-marbling brand pattern, according to a designer portfolio ([Michael Ferrer](https://www.michaelferrerdesign.com/nobu-hotel)). A pattern derived from a craft technique can do a photograph's atmospheric job in a small SVG.
aesthetics.whatToAvoid: Generic 'Japanese minimal' clichés for European properties. Derive patterns from each property's own place.

aesthetics.whatToTake: Proof that premium can be playful: explosive, humorous décor rooted in each neighbourhood, and an uninhibited, generous voice ([Plume Travels](https://plumetravels.com/en/tribu-mama-shelter-lhotellerie-urbaine-au-luxe-impertinent/)). This is a useful counter-direction for restaurants and city hotels: saturated colour fields, a big expressive wordmark, cheeky welcome copy.
aesthetics.whatToAvoid: Neon, clutter and multiple accent colours around the stars. Keep the rating block calm even when the page is loud.

aesthetics.reference: Kinfolk (custom type by Schick Toikka, design by Alex Hunting)
aesthetics.whatToTake: Editorial calm: a custom serif family (text, deck and display) with wedge serifs and lively contrast, a sans for captions, larger body text in the redesign, and deliberately asymmetric whitespace ([It's Nice That](https://www.itsnicethat.com/news/kinfolk-tenth-anniversary-redesign-schick-toikka-publication-graphic-design-230621)). For RepKey: a flush-left question with a generous left margin and a small caps caption can look expensive without a photo.
aesthetics.whatToAvoid: Low-contrast greige text and tiny captions. Editorial softness often fails WCAG.

aesthetics.whatToTake: NN/g attributes the refined look to a monochromatic palette, a limited set of type styles, hierarchy through weight and a strict grid ([NN/g](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/why-does-a-design-look-good-part2/)). This is the clearest evidence that type-only can look premium: one warm paper ground, graphite ink, one serif moment.
aesthetics.whatToAvoid: Copying the recognisable Aesop cream and graphite one to one.

aesthetics.whatToTake: A system of 6 geometric frame shapes per location, taken from local architecture, that can hold photography, illustration, type or plain colour. A modern sans alternates with an elegant serif ([The Brand Identity](https://the-brandidentity.com/project/houston-group-shows-how-hotel-brands-can-be-local-and-consistent)). This is directly useful for RepKey: a frame such as an arch or tile shape can hold a photo later and a colour field today, so the no-photo and photo variants share one layout.
aesthetics.whatToAvoid: Too many shapes on one small screen. Use one frame per portal.

aesthetics.reference: Restaurant identities (Tiago Home Kitchen, The Vandelay, Periplo Portixol)
aesthetics.whatToTake: Huge, unavoidable custom lettering; a warm red and off-white bistro palette; a stencil typeface taken from fishing-boat markings ([The Brand Identity](https://the-brandidentity.com/project/7-restaurant-identities-that-put-the-fine-in-fine-dining-featuring-saint-urbain-dennis-and-more)). For a restaurant variant: a large lowercase wordmark as the hero, plus one appetite colour used only for the accent.
aesthetics.whatToAvoid: A red accent for the selected stars that could read as error or danger. Test the red against error semantics.

aesthetics.whatToTake: A strong sense of place from photography, social and web icons grouped together, and a clear public-review destination.
aesthetics.whatToAvoid: Guests are sent straight to public platforms with no private step. Five filled stars on the platform cards imply the expected score. The hero takes about 55% of the first screen, so the action starts low. The property name appears twice. The language switcher is a flag. Emoji are used as UI. Text sits on busy photos. Hero video costs seconds on hotel wifi.

aesthetics.whatToTake: Ink and champagne, a spaced-caps wordmark, an elegant serif question, outline stars, a privacy line under the button and hairline link rows all fit the research and can be evolved.
aesthetics.whatToAvoid: Digit-only star labels (add word endpoints). The 'Share my rating' label suggests posting publicly. Its look depends on generated resort photography, so it needs a designed no-photo identity strip. The champagne accent must not be reused on a light variant without a darker bronze.

out.typeAndColor:
TYPE. The strongest references pair one characterful display face with one quiet text face. Six Senses uses Canto caps with Avenir Next Condensed ([Fonts In Use](https://fontsinuse.com/uses/36800/six-senses)). Soho House uses a serif with a grotesk. Kinfolk uses a custom wedge serif with a sans for captions. QT Hotels alternates a sans and a serif. Aesop sets almost everything in a grotesk and allows one serif headline (see NN/g). Hard constraint for RepKey: both faces must cover Cyrillic, and ideally the Bulgarian letter forms. Bulgarian Cyrillic differs from the Russian-default shapes, with more ascenders and descenders in the lowercase, and Bulgarian readers notice ([MyFonts / Krista Radoeva](https://www.myfonts.com/a/font/content/cyrillic-script-variations-and-the-importance-of-localisation)). These forms are switched on by the OpenType `locl` feature when the page declares `lang="bg"` ([Lettersoup](https://www.lettersoup.de/what-shall-be-done-for-bulgarian-cyrillic-loclbgr/)). Google Fonts has not added Bulgarian forms across its library; the request is still open ([google/fonts #4745](https://github.com/google/fonts/issues/4745)). Sofia Sans by Lettersoup has Bulgarian forms and 4 width axes, from normal down to extra-condensed ([Sofia Sans](https://fonts.google.com/specimen/Sofia+Sans)). Fira Sans is also reported to include them. Display serifs with Cyrillic, such as Cormorant, Playfair Display and Lora, need per-font checks for `locl` BGR, and a check that the served subset keeps `locl`. Self-host the files if it does not. Suggested scale for 390px screens: question 30–34px display (line-height 1.1, flush-left or centred by direction); body 17px (18px on dark); small caps or labels 12–13px with +6–10% tracking (cap letter-spacing reads fine in Cyrillic too); button 17px medium. Allow for Bulgarian running longer than English and give the question 3 lines.

COLOUR. Use at most 3–4 tokens (NN/g's Aesop analysis) with fixed semantic roles: ground, ink, muted ink, and one accent. The accent is reserved for three things: the selected stars, the primary button and the focus ring. The Google card and the private card share one neutral surface, so no score shows a different colour. Measured contrast checks for this palette family: champagne #C8B48A on ink #111418 is 9.1:1 (passes for stars and button). The same champagne on ivory #F6F1E7 is 1.8:1 (fails 1.4.11), so a light variant needs bronze #8A6D3B (4.31:1). A 'dimmed' #5C6168 unselected star on ink is 2.96:1 (fails; go lighter). Warm off-white text #D9D2C3 on ink is 12.3:1. Evergreen #1F3B2F on ivory is 10.8:1. Champagne on deep green #1B2A22 is 7.4:1. Keep the existing `portal-contrast.ts` luminance picker for text on tenant colours, and add a 3:1 non-text check for star outlines against the surface.

PREMIUM WITHOUT PHOTOGRAPHY (every direction needs this version). (1) An identity strip made of a spaced-caps wordmark or a monogram seal plus a small-caps place line; this was Signature Stay's strongest element. (2) A colour field with fine grain: a pre-rendered tiled noise image or a small data-URI SVG at opacity 0.04–0.08, not a live `feTurbulence` filter, which is costly on mobile ([CSS-Tricks](https://css-tricks.com/grainy-gradients/)). (3) Janu-style hand-dyed gradients tinted per property. (4) A single frame shape (QT / Houston Group) holding a colour field today and a photo later. (5) A pattern taken from local craft or material, like Nobu's ink marbling or Aman's carved marks, as one light SVG. (6) Editorial whitespace and hairline rules (Kinfolk, Aesop) instead of cards and shadows.

THREE DIRECTION SEEDS the research supports, for the direction-synthesis step. (a) 'Carved Stillness': Signature Stay evolved. Ink with champagne, a flared-terminal serif, a monogram and grain, with a bronze-on-ivory light variant. For premium resorts and spas, e.g. Velingrad-type properties. (b) 'Editorial Paper': warm paper and graphite, a grotesk text face with one serif question, hairlines, no chrome. For boutique hotels and cafés. (c) 'Local Colour Field': a per-property saturated field, a frame shape, a big expressive wordmark and warm witty copy (Hoxton, Mama Shelter, restaurant identities). For restaurants and city hotels. All three share the same rating block geometry and the same score-invariant Google card.
out.motion:
PRINCIPLES. Motion should explain cause and effect and stay short. NN/g recommends 100–400ms, entering elements slightly slower than exiting ones, ease-out for entering, and subtler motion for frequent actions ([NN/g animation duration](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/animation-duration/)). Emil Kowalski recommends staying under 300ms, a press scale of about 0.97, never animating from scale(0) (start at 0.9 or more), ease-out easing, and no animation on repeated keyboard actions ([7 tips](https://emilkowal.ski/ui/7-practical-animation-tips), [You don't need animations](https://emilkowal.ski/ui/you-dont-need-animations)). Apple's HIG says motion should be purposeful and optional, never the only carrier of information ([Apple motion](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/motion)). Material 3 puts component animations at 100–300ms and uses decelerate easing for entrances ([M3](https://m3.material.io/styles/motion/easing-and-duration/tokens-specs)). Animate only transform and opacity.

RATING SELECTION. On touch or click, the tapped star presses to scale 0.94 for about 90ms and returns with an ease-out of about 160ms. Stars 1..n fill left to right with a 25ms stagger, capped at about 150ms total. The caption word crossfades over 120ms. The motion must be identical for 1 and for 5: no bigger burst, glow or sparkle for high scores, since unequal celebration implies a preferred answer and moves toward gamification. With the keyboard, arrow-key changes fill instantly with no stagger, because arrows are repeated input.

SUBMIT AND TRANSITION TO THE GOOGLE INVITATION. The button keeps its width and shows 'Sending…'; show an inline progress mark only if the wait passes about 300ms. On success, use a same-document View Transition (Baseline in Chrome, Safari and Firefox 144 since October 2025; [web.dev](https://web.dev/blog/same-document-view-transitions-are-now-baseline-newly-available)), with an instant DOM swap as the fallback. The star row morphs into the one-line receipt over about 280ms, decelerating. The Google card then enters with opacity 0→1 and translateY 8px→0 over about 220ms ease-out, starting about 60ms later. The private-feedback card, when the score is at or below the threshold, uses exactly the same entrance after the Google card, never before it. Focus moves to the new state's heading, and `role=status` announces 'Rating sent privately'.

COMPLETION. Keep it calm: at most a checkmark that draws its stroke (stroke-dashoffset, about 300ms) beside 'Thank you'. No confetti, no star explosions, no counters or streaks; these read as review gamification, which is permanently denied, and they cost frames on low-end phones. When the guest returns from Google, show no motion at all, just the unchanged receipt.

REDUCED MOTION AND PERFORMANCE. Under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, replace all transforms and view transitions with 100ms-or-shorter opacity crossfades or instant swaps. No parallax heroes and no autoplay video (WCAG 2.3.3 context: [Understanding 2.3.3](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/animation-from-interactions.html)). Do not rely on haptics. iOS Safari has never implemented the Vibration API ([MDN](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/API/Vibration_API)), and the checkbox-switch workaround reportedly stopped working in iOS 26.5, so any 'feel' must come from the visual press state. Keep interaction handlers light to stay under the 200ms INP target; set `will-change` only during an animation. No grain animation.

rules.source: Google Maps User Generated Content Policy, 'Prohibited & restricted content' (Fake engagement / Rating manipulation)
rules.rule: Merchants must not 'Discourage or prohibit negative reviews, or selectively solicit positive reviews from customers'. Merchants may solicit genuine reviews 'without offering incentives to do so or attempting to influence the rating or the contents of the review'.
rules.designImplication: The Google action's presence, position, label, size, colour and copy must be the same for a 1-star and a 5-star rating (this matches the invariance rule in ADR 0044). Do not remove, collapse, demote, delay or reword it by score. Do not use copy that steers the rating, such as 'Loved it? Rate us 5 stars on Google' or 'Unhappy? Tell us instead'. Neutral wording is safe: 'Share your experience on Google' or 'Write a review on Google'. Five pre-filled stars on a Google card is an attempt to influence the rating, so do not use them.

rules.source: Google Maps User Generated Content Policy, same page (Incentives, on-premises pressure, staff content)
rules.rule: No incentives (payment, discounts, free goods or services) for posting, revising or removing a review. Merchants 'should not require or pressure users to leave ratings or write reviews while on the premises, nor should they request that specific content be included'. Staff quotas and requests for content that identifies a staff member are also named as violations.
rules.designImplication: Portals are used on the premises (QR on table, NFC at reception), so offering the Google action is fine but pressure is not. Avoid blocking modals, countdowns, 'before you check out' urgency, progress bars toward Google, and celebration tied to the Google click. Never prompt for staff names or topics ('mention Maria', 'tell others about our spa'). No rewards, raffles or discounts anywhere on the page. Placement copy may name the place (for example 'Spa reception') but never a staff member.

rules.source: Google Business Profile Help, 'Tips to get more reviews'
rules.rule: Businesses may ask customers to visit a Google link or scan a QR code. Incentives to post, change or remove reviews are 'strictly prohibited'. The page also says 'A mix of positive and negative feedback often feels more trustworthy' and 'Customers must be signed into a Google Account to leave a review'.
rules.designImplication: A QR code or link that leads to the Google review form is explicitly supported. Add a short honest expectation under the action, for example 'Opens Google Maps. You may need to sign in to Google.' This fits the rule that RepKey only records that the guest selected Google and never claims a review was written. Receipt copy must not say 'Thanks for your Google review'.

rules.source: Google Business Profile Help, 'Business Profile restrictions for policy violations'
rules.rule: If Google finds fake engagement, it can stop a profile from receiving new reviews, unpublish existing reviews for a period, and show consumers a warning that fake reviews were removed.
rules.designImplication: A gating pattern puts the customer's public profile at risk, not only RepKey. This supports making the anti-gating invariance a product guarantee that cannot be configured, rather than a theme option. Admin screens should not offer score-dependent Google visibility or copy.

rules.source: Google Partner Marketing Hub, 'Customer reviews: How to refer to customer ratings and reviews on Google'
rules.rule: Include one of Google's logos (the G or the full wordmark). 'Don't add stars by the Google name or logos.' 'Don't use any unofficial logos, badges, or lockups.' Describe a rating as 'on Google', never as 'Google rating' or 'Google-rated'. Include an 'as of' date when sharing an overall rating or review count. Logos in a group must be the same size.
rules.designImplication: The Ratestar pattern ('Google' plus five gold stars plus 'Rate us') goes against Google's brand guidance. Use the official, unmodified G mark or plain text 'Google', with no stars, invented badges or 'Review us on Google' lockups, and no recolouring of the G to match the theme. If a Tripadvisor action is ever added beside it, the two logos must be the same size. If the property's rating is ever shown, write it as '4.6 on Google, as of 19 Sep 2026' with no star glyphs next to the Google name.

rules.source: Google Business Profile APIs policies (last updated 2026-08-28)
rules.rule: The APIs may be used only 'to create, manage, and report on business listings'. Content may not be pre-fetched, cached or stored except temporarily (30 days or less, stored securely, 'cannot be manipulated or aggregated in any way'). Tools 'must not replicate the look and feel of the Business Profile user interface'. Use of the APIs must not imply partnership, sponsorship or endorsement by Google.
rules.designImplication: The guest portal must not look like Google Maps or a Google review sheet (no Maps-style cards, Google colours or 'Google' styling). No 'Google partner' or 'Verified by Google' badges. The blue verified check in the Ratestar reference implies verification that RepKey cannot provide, so avoid it. Take the review destination from GBP metadata.newReviewUri, as src/contexts/integration/CONTEXT.md already specifies.

rules.source: US FTC Trade Regulation Rule on Consumer Reviews and Testimonials, 16 CFR 465.4 (in effect since 21 Oct 2024)
rules.rule: Businesses may not give compensation or other incentives 'conditioned expressly or by implication on, the writing or creation of consumer reviews expressing a particular sentiment, whether positive or negative'.
